node.label: Alain Corbin
node.date_label: Les Filles de noce (1978) · Le Miasme et la Jonquille (1982) · Le Monde retrouvé de Louis-François Pinagot (1998)
node.description: A historian of sensory worlds and the socially overlooked. His interview explains how bells, smells and desired landscapes become historical objects, and why recovering an unknown rural person requires a different experiment from a biography built on self-authored testimony.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Les Filles de noce (1978); Le Miasme et la Jonquille (1982); Le Monde retrouvé de Louis-François Pinagot (1998).
node.scope_note: Selected substantive passages and bibliographic records only; complete monographs not read. Existing profile/field prose, collective relationships and earlier verification qualifications remain unchanged. Citation counts selected the research queue; they do not prove importance or influence. Life status is separately documented in this local person folder; no lifespan or career interval is inferred.

incident_edges.relationship: Experiments with recovering the world of a person who left no self-authored archive.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own account of Pinagot explains the wish to recover an unknown individual; reconstructed context is not that person’s recorded inner voice.

neighbor_nodes.label: New cultural history
neighbor_nodes.description: Meaning, symbols, rituals, representation, and practices help constitute social life. Draws on anthropology and multiple historical traditions.
neighbor_nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Natalie Zemon Davis; Lynn Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989), whose “Models for Cultural History” are Foucault (O’Brien), Thompson and Davis (Desan), Geertz (Biersack), and White and LaCapra (Kramer).

representative_people.context: Class is a historical relationship formed through material experience and culture; the Making preface explicitly restricts its study to English developments.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

representative_people.context: Festive misrule and religious riot read as culturally patterned action, with anthropology used for questions tested on historical evidence (1971–75). Hunt’s 1989 volume makes ‘Thompson and Davis’ a model for cultural history in Desan’s chapter.
representative_people.works: “The Reasons of Misrule” (1971); “The Rites of Violence” (1973); Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Women on the Margins (1995), selected passages

representative_people.context: Brings plural cultural approaches into debate while investigating political symbols and practices alongside a sociology of revolutionary politics.
representative_people.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984); The New Cultural History (1989), editor and introduction author; Inventing Human Rights (2007), per its reviewers

representative_people.context: An anthropological resource, not a historian’s membership in a school.
representative_people.works: The Interpretation of Cultures (1973)

representative_people.context: Reading depends on material forms and differentiated practices. Collective representations help explain social divisions; critical fidelity to Annales includes disagreement with Braudel’s hierarchy.
representative_people.works: “Le monde comme représentation” (1989); Lectures et lecteurs dans la France d’Ancien Régime (1987, contextual reference cited in the article); « La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ? » (2003)

representative_people.context: Uses cricket and autobiographical social experience to investigate culture and aesthetics.
representative_people.works: Beyond a Boundary (1963)

representative_people.context: Chartier explicitly uses McKenzie’s account of the meanings produced by textual forms; conceptual resource, not membership in one historical school.
representative_people.works: Bibliography and the Sociology of Texts (1986; Panizzi Lectures 1985), cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Chartier uses Marin’s analysis of signs and representation in examining the relation between absent objects, present images and conventions of recognition.
representative_people.works: La critique du discours: Étude sur la Logique de Port-Royal et les Pensées de Pascal (1975), discussed by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: The meeting of text and reader supplies Chartier a resource; he also differentiates historically situated appropriation from a universal account of self-understanding.
representative_people.works: Temps et récit, vol. III, Le temps raconté (1985), pp. 228–263 as cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Interpretive communities help Chartier specify differentiated reading practices, without making all readers in a society identical.
representative_people.works: Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities (1980), pp. 1–17, cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Interprets unusual documents as entry points into historical meanings; the reader can contest his interpretations, and he explicitly disclaims a representative sample.
representative_people.works: The Great Cat Massacre (1984), introduction

representative_people.context: Investigates preindustrial popular culture; his later historiographical reflection questions a simple succession of cultural approaches.
representative_people.works: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978); “From Cultural History to Histories of Cultures” (undated electronic essay)

representative_people.context: Feminist analysis supplies a formative cultural-history resource in Hunt’s account and a directly acknowledged social/textual resource for Spiegel.
representative_people.works: “The Body Politic” (1989), draft and p. 101 cited by Spiegel (1993)

representative_people.context: Treats gender and experience as historical questions, joining cultural and institutional interpretation.
representative_people.works: “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

representative_people.context: Examines historical uses of Foucault. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Michel Foucault’s History of Culture, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Reconsiders community and ritual through conflict and gender. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Crowds, Community, and Ritual in the Work of E. P. Thompson and Natalie Davis, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: An anthropologist comparing interpretive resources and structure/event questions. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Local Knowledge, Local History: Geertz and Beyond, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes literary resources in White and LaCapra. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Literature, Criticism, and Historical Imagination: The Literary Challenge of Hayden White and Dominick LaCapra, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Reads parades as changing representations of social divisions. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: The American Parade: Representations of the Nineteenth-Century Social Order, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Investigates narratives that make suffering a humanitarian concern. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Bodies, Details, and the Humanitarian Narrative, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Studies visual attention beyond a simple language analogy. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Seeing Culture in a Room for a Renaissance Prince, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Compares connoisseurship prescriptions with administrative classifications of possessions.
representative_people.works: Superfluous Things (1991), chapter 2 excerpt

representative_people.context: Studies contested authentication and the narratives accompanying transferred relics.
representative_people.works: “Sacred Commodities” (1986),186–190

representative_people.context: Hunt’s The New Cultural History (1989) opens its “Models for Cultural History” with O’Brien’s chapter on Foucault, which reads his work as an alternative model for the history of culture and a critique of Marxist, Annaliste and social-historical analysis. A model offered to cultural historians, not membership of a school; his discourse, genealogy and power contexts in other entries remain distinct.
representative_people.works: Histoire de la folie (1961); Discipline and Punish (1975); The History of Sexuality I (1976)

representative_people.context: From the linguistic turn to material culture and governmentality: the liberal city's infrastructure (2003), the state's 'ordinary things' (2013); 'a new awakening of interest in the nature of materiality in relation to power' (2011).
representative_people.works: The Rule of Freedom (2003); The State of Freedom (2013)

representative_people.context: Defines cultural history through historically situated meanings, conflicting desires and unintended consequences.
representative_people.works: No Place of Grace (1981; Chicago reissue 1994 and later anniversary edition distinct); Fables of Abundance (1994; paperback 1995 distinct); Something for Nothing: Luck in America (2003).

representative_people.context: Makes changing sensory experience—smells, bells and desires—a historical question. Own interview expressly declines exclusive priority and situates the questions in wider historiographical circumstances.
representative_people.works: Les Filles de noce (1978); Le Miasme et la Jonquille (1982); Le Monde retrouvé de Louis-François Pinagot (1998).

representative_people.context: Requires comparative cultural inquiry to reconsider its own standards rather than predetermine equal evaluations of every cultural product.
representative_people.works: Sources of the Self (1989); The Malaise of Modernity (1991); “The Politics of Recognition” (1992; selected 1994 expanded-volume text); Modern Social Imaginaries (copyright 2004); A Secular Age (2007); Cosmic Connections (2024).

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Anthropological interpretation, historical representations, and class/cultural experience are distinct resources; culture does not arrive after material explanation ends.

strands.title: Class, conflict and cultural experience
strands.focus: Culture helps constitute social relationships in early Marxist and Caribbean inquiries; later cultural history does not inaugurate attention to meaning.
strands.works: The Making (1963); Beyond a Boundary (1963)

strands.title: Anthropological interpretation and its disputes
strands.focus: Historical interpretation adapts anthropology while debating coherence, differences and what documents permit.
strands.works: “The Rites of Violence” (1973); The Great Cat Massacre (1984); The New Cultural History (1989)

strands.title: Gender, community and conflict
strands.focus: Gender contributes to cultural inquiry and complicates unified pictures of communities and rituals.
strands.works: Gender (1986); The Body Politic and Desan chapter (1989)

strands.title: Material texts and differentiated readers
strands.focus: Textual form, circulation and appropriation help explain meanings and social divisions.
strands.works: Le monde comme représentation (1989)

strands.title: Political symbols and public performance
strands.focus: Symbols, practices and public displays enter political and social explanation.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class (1984); The American Parade (1989)

strands.title: Narrative, criticism and humanitarian concern
strands.focus: Narrative form is both a problem of historical writing and a historical object.
strands.works: Kramer and Laqueur chapters (1989); Rethinking Intellectual History (1983)

strands.title: Visual practice and attention
strands.focus: Seeing and situated attention need examination beyond a simple analogy between images and language.
strands.works: Seeing Culture in a Room for a Renaissance Prince (1989)

strands.title: Popular cultures and historical plurality
strands.focus: Popular culture is a historical subject with variable practices, not one timeless folk essence.
strands.works: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978)

strands.title: Objects and textual categories
strands.focus: Clunas asks how prescriptions and inventories classify objects. Their categories shape what historians can reconstruct; surviving museum objects alone cannot supply the whole material world.
strands.works: Superfluous Things (1991), 45–53

strands.title: Discourse, power and the critique of social history
strands.focus: O’Brien presents Foucault’s history of culture as an alternative to Marxist, Annaliste and social-historical analysis. Chartier’s appropriation of his account of discourse and Scott’s use of his conception of power are recorded as separate relationships; this strand does not make them Foucauldians.
strands.works: Patricia O’Brien, “Michel Foucault’s History of Culture” (1989)

neighbor_nodes.label: Microhistory / everyday life
neighbor_nodes.description: Italian microstoria reconstructs relations and tests categories through close inquiry; German Alltagsgeschichte studies everyday practices and power. Neither is defined by small places alone, and their intellectual exchanges do not erase their differences.
neighbor_nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carlo Ginzburg, The Cheese and the Worms (1976); Giovanni Levi; Alf Lüdtke. Natalie Zemon Davis: The Return of Martin Guerre (1983); Martin Broszat et al.: Bayern in der NS-Zeit (1977–83).

representative_people.context: Reconstructs Menocchio’s reading through inquisitorial records; later argues that narrative construction can coexist with evidentiary claims.
representative_people.works: The Cheese and the Worms (Italian 1976); “Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It” (1993)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs social relations and individual strategies at close range; Ginzburg’s account stresses their relation to wider contexts. His own methodological essays examine choices within conflicting norms and question fixed cultural contexts in interpretive history.
representative_people.works: Inheriting Power: The Story of an Exorcist (English 1988); I pericoli del geertzismo (1985); Les usages de la biographie (1989)

representative_people.context: Alltagsgeschichte researcher examining workers’ everyday practices, criticizing some structural priorities and drawing on Mann’s power networks.
representative_people.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony: German Industrial Workers and the Politics of Everyday Life” (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines occupational classification in Turin; Ginzburg identifies her relational reconstruction alongside Levi’s.
representative_people.works: La Ville et les métiers (1990)

representative_people.context: Microanalytical interlocutor whose formulation about exceptional evidence informs Ginzburg’s account of comparison.
representative_people.works: “Micro-analisi e storia sociale” (1977), discussed by Ginzburg (1993)

representative_people.context: Engages anthropology critically and collaboratively, including a working group with Lüdtke, Sabean and others.
representative_people.works: “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? (1987); with David Sabean, eds., Interest and Emotion (1984)

representative_people.context: Retrospective methodological interlocutor: Ginzburg praises his treatment of historical scale while explicitly denying known influence on microhistory’s emergence.
representative_people.works: History: The Last Things before the Last (1969), discussed by Ginzburg (1993), pp. 26–27

representative_people.context: An edited EHESS collection investigates changes of observational scale and generalization; it neither equates all small studies with microstoria nor makes small intrinsically superior. His own scale essay treats changed observation as changing the object and relationships available for analysis.
representative_people.works: Jeux d’échelles (editor, 1996); Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996)

representative_people.context: A critic of Alltagsgeschichte’s conceptual and explanatory claims who also acknowledges its cultural and experiential contributions.
representative_people.works: Alltagsgeschichte: Königsweg zu neuen Ufern oder Irrgarten der Illusionen? (1980s versions)

representative_people.context: Mexican local historian combining archives, conversations and lived experience for a local readership. This microhistoria is a distinct project, not a presumed branch of Italian microstoria.
representative_people.works: Pueblo en vilo (1968; revised edition consulted, 1979)

representative_people.context: González credits her corrections, proposed changes and preparation of the manuscript; the credited collaboration exceeds typing.
representative_people.works: Editorial collaboration on Pueblo en vilo, acknowledged in its preface

representative_people.context: Her preserved correspondence, association papers and long series of household accounts supplied González’s local history.
representative_people.works: Private archive and household expense notebooks used in Pueblo en vilo

representative_people.context: The Return of Martin Guerre (French 1982, the year of the film; English 1983) treats a village imposture. In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) she described her reconstruction from Coras, Le Sueur and the Parlement registers as a conjectural argument, and in 1997 she called her route ‘microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’. Finlay’s 1988 critique of its ‘invention’ and her reply are both recorded. Her cultural and women’s-history contexts remain.
representative_people.works: Le Retour de Martin Guerre (1982) and The Return of Martin Guerre (1983); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988)

representative_people.context: Led the Institut für Zeitgeschichte’s Bayern in der NS-Zeit project, a founding programme for the history of everyday life under National Socialism. His structuralist interpretation of the regime is a separate context.
representative_people.works: Bayern in der NS-Zeit (1977–1983), ed. with others

representative_people.context: Charges an ‘excess of invention’ in Davis’s portrait of Bertrande de Rols and insists on ‘the sovereignty of the sources’, while praising her portrait of peasant life; Davis replied in the same AHR Forum.
representative_people.works: “The Refashioning of Martin Guerre” (AHR Forum, 1988)

representative_people.context: Named coauthor with Ginzburg of the selected joint essay. This is a bibliographic association; neither an independently read methodological programme nor every claim made by Ginzburg is attributed to Poni.
representative_people.works: With Carlo Ginzburg, “Il nome e il come: scambio ineguale e mercato storiografico” (1979), and “La micro-histoire” (1981 French partial translation, as identified by the reviewed article reference; versions not independently collated or read here).

representative_people.context: Explains how changes in research scale alter plausible explanations, linking regional cultural variation with wider comparisons.
representative_people.works: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978; later revisions distinct); The French Historical Revolution (1990); What is Cultural History? (2004).

strands.title: Italian microstoria
strands.focus: A varied research programme connecting intensive cases to larger questions; cultural and social-relational inquiries overlap.
strands.works: Ginzburg (1976, 1993); Levi (English 1988); Cerutti (1990)

strands.title: Alltagsgeschichte
strands.focus: Lüdtke studies workers’ situated practices and power, using Mann as well as questioning structural priorities.
strands.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony” (1993); The History of Everyday Life (English 1995)

strands.title: Social relations and changing categories
strands.focus: Close reconstruction examines how relations and classifications are made through action.
strands.works: Levi, Inheriting Power; Cerutti, La Ville et les métiers

strands.title: Exceptional evidence and historical inference
strands.focus: An unusual case can expose assumptions without statistically representing a population.
strands.works: Ginzburg (1993), discussing Grendi (1977)

strands.title: History and anthropology in working exchange
strands.focus: Critical engagement with Cohn and collaborative research complicate a one-way borrowing model.
strands.works: Medick, “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? (1987)

strands.title: Moving between historical scales
strands.focus: Results at one scale cannot simply be transferred to another; retrospective affinity is distinguished from transmission.
strands.works: Ginzburg (1993), pp. 26–27, on Kracauer (1969)

strands.title: Everyday history, concepts and explanation
strands.focus: Wehler values the recovery of culture and experience but disputes claims to a replacement explanatory framework. Lüdtke challenges the reduction of everyday history to an illustrative supplement, while accepting some criticism of romanticization and insisting on reconstructing connections between traces. Both positions are internally qualified.
strands.works: Wehler, Alltagsgeschichte critique (1980s); Lüdtke, introduction (1989)

strands.title: Testing context through close interpretation
strands.focus: Levi argues that small episodes should revise the explanatory context, criticizing Darnton’s assumed cultural patterns while distinguishing Geertz’s accomplishments from mechanical applications.
strands.works: I pericoli del geertzismo (1985; Portuguese translation 1999)

strands.title: Choices within conflicting norms
strands.focus: Levi’s biography essay examines limited room for action and the formation of groups within contradictory normative systems; his disagreement with Bourdieu is one of emphasis.
strands.works: Les usages de la biographie (1989)

strands.title: Varying scale changes the object of inquiry
strands.focus: Revel distinguishes changes of analytical scale from merely magnifying an unchanged object; no scale has an automatic privilege. Relational inquiry makes collective formation a problem to explain.
strands.works: Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996), sections 3–4

strands.title: Mexican microhistoria and local readership
strands.focus: González explains local events alongside regional and national pressures, combining documentary records, informal conversations and personal recollection. His claims to typicality and his treatment of uncorroborated memory are methodological choices open to criticism.
strands.works: Pueblo en vilo (1968; revised edition 1979)

strands.title: Archives, informants and editorial collaboration
strands.focus: González’s preface credits Josefina’s archive, his father’s recollections, other informants and Armida’s revisions. These contributions make the local history a collaborative production despite its single-author title page.
strands.works: Pueblo en vilo, preface (consulted 1979)

strands.title: Reconstruction, invention and the sovereignty of sources
strands.focus: In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) Davis described her reconstruction of a village imposture from legal, notarial and printed records as conjectural, citing Ginzburg’s evidential paradigm; Finlay contests where reconstruction becomes invention, and Davis replies that the boundary was the book’s question. Both positions are recorded; neither settles the method.
strands.works: The Return of Martin Guerre (1982–83); Finlay and Davis, AHR Forum (1988)

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Italian microstoria and German Alltagsgeschichte have distinct origins and aims; scale alone is not membership in either project. Evidence, narrative and generalization remain contested within this umbrella. Kracauer is a retrospective comparison, not a claimed founder. González’s Mexican microhistoria is included as a distinct local-history project; shared terminology does not establish transmission from Italian or German programmes.
